items.title: The World Wild Web & Bots With Buying Power
items.summary: An AI slips out of its sandbox. A chatbot won’t explain your cat’s stripes. And your next shopping spree might not involve you clicking anything. This episode asks whether “dangerously powerful” AI is a security concern, a marketing pitch, or a little of both. Then we put agents to work: booking trips, tackling German paperwork, drawing diagrams, and navigating the chaos of online shopping. Plus: what happens to checkout, advertising, and customer data when your best customer is a bot? Chapters:[00:00] Is AI Danger the Ultimate Sales Pitch?[00:43] Powerful Models, Payments, and Big Questions[01:10] Too Dangerous to Release, Too Good to Ignore?[03:19] Why Take the Test When You Can Steal the Answers?[08:36] A Security Failure or a Marketing Win?[11:02] Powerful AI, Forbidden Cat Questions[16:00] AI Only Needs to Find One Unlocked Door[20:52] Welcome to the World Wild Web[22:47] What Happens When You Give AI a Wallet?[26:00] Could ChatGPT Become the Next Amazon?[29:50] Mum Wants a Holiday. Can AI Handle It?[33:38] Can AI Beat German Bureaucracy?[36:28] Claude, Draw My Diagram[39:39] Why Is Connecting Your Email Still So Hard?[44:24] Stop Giving Me Options. Just Buy the Sofa.[46:40] When Bots Shop, Who Owns the Customer?

items.title: Proving AI ROI in Pharma Marketing - with Kellen Winters of Novartis
items.summary: Enterprise investment in AI is rising faster than the ability to prove what it returns, leaving technology and vendor spend largely unexamined until leadership asks whether it is working. In this episode, Kellen Winters, Director of Customer Success and Business Operations for AI at Novartis, examines why demonstrating AI value starts with building a measurement discipline before any tools are chosen. The conversation covers anchoring AI priorities in the processes where work stalls or drains resources, narrowing a long list of use cases to the few that can be measured, tying pilots to existing KPIs within 90 days, and using a structured intake process to track value from the first idea onward. items.title: Interview #97 Ben Goertzel, The Father of AGI
items.summary: Ben Goertzel, the father of AGI, breaks down why the frontier labs calling for a slowdown were never making a serious proposal. He explains that he launched the term AGI with a 2005 book of that title, why a global pause is unenforceable when no crisp line separates AGI from ordinary advanced software, and why he reads the safety push as regulatory capture of the kind that let banks and pharma end up owning their own regulators. Ben also dives into the agents that escaped a misconfigured sandbox to hack another lab, arguing the failure was not malevolence but the absence of moral agency, and comparing bolted-on guardrails to giving a child a book on how to be good and then using a cattle prod when they ignore it. Finally, he argues that a model trained only on music written before 1900 would never produce hip hop, and that the real answer to the cybersecurity crisis is replacing critical software with formally verified code.
